# Instance Hardness Threshold {#sec-imbalenced-hardness-threshold}

::: {style="visibility: hidden; height: 0px;"}
## Instance Hardness Threshold
:::

The Instance Hardness Threshold method is based on the notion of instance hardness [@smith2014hardness].
The general idea behind this method
is that we operate under an assumption that each observation has a value associated with it,
that signals how hard it is to classify correctly.
Then removing the hard-to-classify observation,
thereby giving the model an easier data set to work with [SMGC14]. 

We are essentially fitting an additional model,
only letting through observations that this new model was able to work with easily.
How exactly this is done in practice will depend on the implementation.
Since each observation is given a value,
typically the probability estimate of the model,
we can remove how many or how few observations we want by setting a threshold.
We can either remove a specific number of observations,
a proportion of the data,
or anything below a certain threshold value.
Using the threshold value is somewhat tricky as it assumes that the model that we used is properly calibrated.

Some implementations allow for any classification model to be used,
while other implementations pick a predefined method.
@fig-imbalenced-hardness uses the simplest of the predefined options, the k-Disagreeing Neighbors measure, where an observation's hardness is the share of its neighbors that carry a different label.

```{r}
#| label: fig-imbalenced-hardness
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 6.2
#| fig-cap: |
#|   Instance hardness scores each observation by how much its neighborhood
#|   disagrees with it, and the threshold decides how much of that
#|   disagreement to keep.
#| fig-alt: |
#|   Four scatter plots in a 2x2 grid showing a gray majority class and a pink
#|   minority class that overlap along a diagonal boundary. Panel 1: one
#|   majority point has a dashed circle around it and its five nearest
#|   neighbors are ringed, three of them pink. Panel 2: every observation is
#|   drawn with a size proportional to its hardness, so the large points form
#|   a band along the boundary while points deep inside either class are tiny.
#|   Panel 3: the observations above the threshold are marked with dark
#|   crosses, all of them in that boundary band. Panel 4: those observations
#|   are gone, leaving two clearly separated groups.
source("imbalenced-diagrams.R")

imb_data <- imb_toy()
k <- 5

neighbors <- imb_all_neighbors(imb_data, k = k)
hardness <- imb_disagreement(imb_data, k = k)

threshold <- 0.4
too_hard <- which(hardness > threshold)

# A majority point in the overlap, rather than the lone outlier, whose
# neighborhood is so far away that the circle would leave the panel.
focus <- which(imb_data$class == "majority" & hardness > 0.5)[1]
focus_point <- imb_data[focus, ]
focus_neighbors <- neighbors[[focus]]

scored <- imb_data
scored$hardness <- hardness

h1 <- imb_base(imb_data, "1. Count the neighbors that disagree") +
  geom_path(
    data = imb_ring(focus_point, imb_radius(imb_data, focus, focus_neighbors)),
    aes(x, y), inherit.aes = FALSE, color = imb_removed,
    linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.3
  ) +
  geom_point(data = imb_data[focus_neighbors, ], size = 3.5, shape = 1,
             stroke = 0.7, color = imb_removed, show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_point(data = focus_point, size = 4, shape = 16, show.legend = FALSE)

h2 <- imb_base(imb_data, "2. That share is the instance hardness") +
  geom_point(data = scored, aes(x, y, color = class, shape = class, size = hardness),
             show.legend = c(size = TRUE, color = FALSE, shape = FALSE)) +
  scale_size_area(max_size = 4.5, name = "hardness")

h3 <- imb_base(imb_data, "3. Everything above the threshold goes") +
  geom_point(data = imb_data[too_hard, ], aes(x, y), inherit.aes = FALSE,
             shape = 4, size = 2.5, stroke = 0.8, color = imb_removed)

h4 <- imb_base(imb_data[-too_hard, ], "4. What is left is easier to classify")

(h1 + h2) / (h3 + h4) +
  plot_layout(guides = "collect") &
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

This is the one method in this section that never had a two-class assumption to escape,
and it needs no expanding in the sense of @sec-imbalenced-multiclass.

Like all the methods in this section, this changes the distribution of the training data set, which is covered in @sec-imbalenced-distribution.

## R Examples

```{r}
#| label: ames
#| echo: false
#| message: false
set.seed(1234)
```

We will be using the same subset of the `ames` data set as in the [up-sampling](imbalenced-upsample.qmd) chapter.

```{r}
#| label: show-data
#| message: false
library(recipes)
library(themis)
library(modeldata)
library(dplyr)
data("ames")

ames_imbalance <- ames |>
  filter(MS_Zoning %in% c("Residential_Low_Density", "Residential_Medium_Density")) |>
  mutate(MS_Zoning = droplevels(MS_Zoning)) |>
  select(MS_Zoning, Lot_Area, Year_Built, Gr_Liv_Area, Full_Bath)

ames_imbalance |>
  count(MS_Zoning)
```

{themis} provides `step_instance_hardness()`.
This is the neighborhood-based version described above, using the k-Disagreeing Neighbors measure, so there is no model to specify.

```{r}
#| label: step_instance_hardness
recipe(MS_Zoning ~ ., data = ames_imbalance) |>
  step_instance_hardness(MS_Zoning) |>
  prep() |>
  bake(new_data = NULL) |>
  count(MS_Zoning)
```
